description: Cells exposed to changing extracellular salt must defend their volume and internal ion balance or lose enzyme function and membrane integrity; the cellular response to salt stress is the set of adjustments that follow such a change. It matters most in tissues that routinely face osmotic swings, above all the kidney medulla, where interstitial sodium and urea reach concentrations that would kill most cells. The genes here span the main arms of that defence: aldose reductase generates sorbitol as a compatible osmolyte, aquaporin-1 provides regulated water flux, a potassium-chloride cotransporter and the sodium pump gamma subunit tune ion movement, and the mechanosensitive channel TRPV4 reports cell swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components and LETM1 link osmotic and ionic stress to organelle homeostasis, while transcript-stability and DNA-repair factors handle the downstream consequences of hypertonic damage.

When nitric oxide or peroxynitrite accumulates, proteins become S-nitrosylated and tyrosine-nitrated and DNA is damaged; the cellular response to nitrosative stress is the set of adaptations that let a cell survive or die cleanly under those conditions. It matters most in inflamed tissue and in neurons, where sustained nitric oxide output from activated glia contributes to neurodegeneration, and it is one reason macrophage-derived NO is toxic to bystander cells. The genes here connect several arms of that defence: PARK7/DJ-1 acts as a redox-sensitive protector whose loss causes early-onset parkinsonism, DNAJA1 provides chaperone support for misfolded and modified proteins, autophagic turnover through ATG5 clears damaged cargo, ATM couples nitrosative DNA lesions to checkpoint signalling, and DDIT3/CHOP links persistent stress to apoptotic commitment. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of proteostasis, genome surveillance and inflammatory injury.

Hydroperoxides, the monosubstituted relatives of hydrogen peroxide, arise from lipid and membrane oxidation, and cells must sense them and respond by changing gene expression, redox enzyme output, survival signalling or growth arrest. The cellular response to hydroperoxide covers that adaptation, which sets the threshold between tolerated oxidative stress and oxidant-driven death, and is relevant to atherosclerosis, where oxidised lipoproteins taken up by scavenger receptors such as CD36 deliver the oxidant load. Detoxification capacity is supplied by glutathione transferase activity in membranes, while oxidation resistance factors and p53-induced stress genes bias the outcome toward antioxidant defence or apoptosis. Kinases including PRKCD and DAPK1 transduce the oxidant signal into death and cytoskeletal programmes, and chromatin corepressor activity links it to transcriptional reprogramming. Together these place peroxide handling at the junction of lipid metabolism, redox homeostasis and stress-induced cell fate decisions.

Cellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle triggered by telomere erosion, oncogene activation or persistent damage, and this pathway covers the mechanisms that hold it off so that proliferating and stem-like cells retain their capacity to divide. Telomerase components, including the catalytic subunit TERT and its RNA template TERC, together with the telomere-protective factor TERF2, prevent chromosome ends from being read as damage; the sirtuins SIRT1 and SIRT6 act as NAD-dependent deacetylases restraining damage and stress responses at chromatin. Transcriptional repressors such as BCL6, TBX2 and TWIST1 suppress the p16/p21 arrest programme, while CDK6 and cell-cycle regulators drive continued proliferation and several microRNAs damp senescence-promoting transcripts. Losing this restraint contributes to tissue ageing and stem cell exhaustion; its excess allows damaged cells to escape the senescence barrier to tumour formation.

Cells exposed to oxidative or genotoxic insult — hydrogen peroxide, irradiation — can exit the cycle permanently rather than repair and divide, and stress-induced premature senescence is that irreversible arrest. It limits the propagation of damaged genomes and so acts as a barrier to tumour formation, but the accumulation of such arrested cells in tissues contributes to ageing phenotypes and chronic inflammation. The route runs through p38 MAPK and its downstream kinase relaying stress signals to p53, which induces the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 to lock the cell out of S phase. Modifiers set the threshold: the deacetylase SIRT1 restrains p53 activity and is protective against oxidative arrest, while a secreted WNT contributes to the paracrine phenotype of senescent cells. A circadian transcription factor links the response to metabolic and redox rhythms.

Cells monitor leucine because it is the amino acid that most strongly licenses growth, and the cellular response to leucine starvation is how they stand down anabolism when it runs short. When leucine is abundant, sestrins release the GATOR2 complex and leucyl-tRNA synthetase and the Rag GTPases permit mTORC1 to dock at the lysosome; withdrawal reverses this, mTORC1 activity falls, protein synthesis and ribosome biogenesis are curtailed, and autophagy is de-repressed to recover amino acids from bulk cytoplasm. In parallel, uncharged tRNA accumulation drives a transcriptional arm through ATF4 and ATF2 that induces amino acid transporters, synthetases and stress-adaptive genes, including the sestrins themselves as a feedback loop. This surveillance couples nutrient supply to cell size, muscle protein balance and immune cell activation, and is the route by which leucine and its analogues influence mTOR-dependent growth control.

Oxygen above normal tension is toxic, and cells respond to hyperoxia with a defined programme of stress signalling, antioxidant and clearance responses, and, when damage exceeds repair, death. This matters most in the lung, where supplemental oxygen given to preterm infants and ventilated patients injures alveolar epithelium and endothelium, contributing to bronchopulmonary dysplasia and acute lung injury. Raised oxygen drives reactive species production, with NADPH oxidase activity adding superoxide to the burden, while the FOXO1 transcription factor redirects gene expression toward stress resistance and apoptosis. Death receptor signalling through FAS commits irreversibly damaged cells to apoptosis, and autophagy machinery requiring ATG7 clears oxidised proteins and damaged mitochondria, a response that can protect or contribute to cell loss. Caveolin-1 links the membrane compartment to these decisions. The balance between adaptation and death determines tissue outcome.

Cells exposed to a solute concentration higher than their own shrink as water leaves, and the cellular hyperosmotic response is how they sense that loss and restore volume and ionic balance. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where interstitial osmolality is extreme by design, and its failure leaves cells with concentrated intracellular salt, protein damage and DNA breaks. Two arms dominate the gene list. A kinase cascade in which WNK1 and WNK3 activate the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 switches on electroneutral cation-chloride transport to reaccumulate ions, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives expression of organic osmolyte machinery, including aldose reductase for sorbitol synthesis, so that volume can be regained without raising intracellular ionic strength. Aquaporin-mediated water flux, glucose uptake, mitochondrial calcium and magnesium handling, and cytoskeletal remodelling through ARHGEF2 accompany the adaptation.

When oxygen falls, mitochondria are primed to release apoptogenic factors, and this set describes the braking mechanisms that block that hypoxia-induced intrinsic apoptotic route so cells survive ischaemia rather than die. It matters in tissues that routinely experience low oxygen or transient ischaemia — heart, brain, kidney — where such restraint limits infarct size, and in solid tumours, where the same protection lets hypoxic cells persist and resist therapy. The mechanisms are varied: survival signalling through PI3K and MEK sustains anti-apoptotic gene expression, an ARC-type inhibitor blocks caspase activation, an ER stress-inducible chaperone and a transmembrane BAX inhibitor buffer calcium release and mitochondrial permeabilisation, and PINK1 preserves mitochondrial quality control and membrane integrity. Metabolic adaptation is part of the response as well, linking glycolytic enzyme function to survival under oxygen limitation.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a by-product of aerobic metabolism and a deliberate second messenger, and this pathway covers how a cell senses it and reshapes its behaviour in response. The outcome ranges from restored redox balance to inflammation, growth arrest and regulated death, so it sits at the heart of oxidative stress biology in ageing, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Detoxification and thiol buffering by catalase, thioredoxin and PARK7 limit the signal, while NFE2L2 drives the antioxidant transcriptional programme and SIRT1 and histone-modifying enzymes tune the longer-term response. Peroxide-sensitive kinases including SRC, ABL1, PRKCD and MAP3K5 relay the stimulus, RELA links it to cytokine output such as IL6, and TRPM2 and TRPA1 convert it into calcium and sensory signals. When damage exceeds repair, autophagy, mitochondrial permeability transition and RIPK1/RIPK3 necroptosis are engaged instead.

When glucose runs low, cells must switch from growth and biosynthesis to conservation and self-digestion, and this starvation response is what makes that switch. It preserves ATP levels and viability during ischaemia, exercise and nutrient-poor tumour microenvironments, and its failure leaves cells unable to survive metabolic stress. Falling energy charge activates the AMP-activated kinase complex through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, which restrains anabolic signalling and licenses autophagy via the class III PI3-kinase complex containing beclin 1, VPS34 and ATG14. In parallel, the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response drives ATF4 to induce amino-acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, while sestrins, FOXO3, p53 and SIRT1 reinforce catabolic and antioxidant programmes. Glucose and amino acid transporters, GATOR/KICSTOR components and lipid droplet perilipins tie nutrient sensing to mTORC1 control and to mobilisation of internal fuel stores.

Cells sense falling oxygen and respond by remodelling metabolism, survival and gene expression; this pathway covers inputs that amplify that response, making the hypoxic programme stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone would produce. Such positive regulation matters in ischaemic tissue, in the hypoxic cores of solid tumours, and in pulmonary and neuronal adaptation to low oxygen, where the size of the response determines whether a cell adapts or dies. The contributing genes are heterogeneous rather than a single complex: a de novo DNA methyltransferase links hypoxia to epigenetic reprogramming, a two-pore potassium channel and a metabotropic glutamate receptor connect membrane excitability and neurotransmitter signalling to oxygen stress, and two microRNAs tune the downstream transcript pool. Together they act as modifiers upstream of hypoxia-inducible transcription and its metabolic, angiogenic and apoptotic outputs.

Cellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle imposed on damaged, stressed or oncogene-activated cells, and this pathway covers the inputs that push cells into that state. It acts as a barrier to tumour formation — mutant KRAS signalling, for example, triggers senescence rather than transformation unless the programme is disabled — while its chronic activation drives tissue ageing and the inflammatory secretory phenotype of aged tissue. TP53 sits at the centre, supported by effectors such as YPEL3 and PAWR, and by cytosolic DNA sensing through CGAS, which links damaged chromatin fragments to an interferon-flavoured arrest. Several microRNAs, notably MIR34A and MIR22, reinforce the decision by silencing proliferative and survival targets, and SIRT1 appears here as a deacetylase whose modulation tunes the p53 response. The output is durable growth arrest with altered secretion and immune visibility.

Cells placed in a hypotonic environment take up water and swell, and the cellular hypotonic response is how they sense that swelling and restore volume before the membrane or cytoskeleton is damaged. It matters for epithelial fluid secretion, corneal and lens transparency, renal water handling and nociceptor mechanosensitivity; loss of its components causes corneal endothelial dystrophy, neuropathy and skeletal dysplasias. Mechanism begins with detection of membrane stretch and dilution, notably through the stretch-sensitive cation channel TRPV4 and water flux via aquaporin channels, and continues as solutes leave the cell through chloride and potassium-chloride cotransport pathways such as CLCN2 and SLC12A6, driving regulatory volume decrease. The WNK-activated kinases OXSR1 and STK39 with their scaffold CAB39 set cotransporter phosphorylation according to tonicity, while myosin light chain kinase links volume change to cytoskeletal tension.

Hydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can push cells past a threshold into programmed death, and this pathway describes the braking mechanisms that keep them alive. It matters wherever cells face chronic oxidant load: cardiomyocytes after ischaemia, dopaminergic neurons, and tissues undergoing regeneration, where premature death would mean irreplaceable loss. Survival signalling through the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET converges on AKT1 to suppress apoptotic commitment, while the scaffold RACK1 and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrain death machinery at the organelle. PARK7 and PINK1, both mutated in recessive parkinsonism, protect mitochondria from oxidative damage and support removal of damaged ones, linking failure of this protection to neurodegeneration. Several microRNAs, including miR-21 and members of the miR-17/92 and let-7 families, tune the same survival programmes post-transcriptionally, and carbonic anhydrase 3 contributes antioxidant buffering in muscle.

Hydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can permeabilize mitochondria and commit a cell to death, and this pathway covers the controls that set how readily that happens. Tuning it decides whether a transient burst of peroxide is buffered or converted into caspase activation, which matters for neuronal survival, muscle and cardiac tolerance of ischaemia, and the resistance of tumour cells to oxidative therapy. Most of the components act as brakes: AKT1 signalling promotes survival, PARK7 and PINK1 protect mitochondria against oxidative damage and their loss causes recessive Parkinson's disease, and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrains permeabilization. RACK1 scaffolds the kinases involved, carbonic anhydrase III contributes antioxidant thiol capacity, and two microRNAs add post-transcriptional regulation. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of redox homeostasis and the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis rather than within either alone.

Hydrogen peroxide accumulating inside a cell can either be detoxified or read as a death signal, and this pathway covers the inputs that push the balance toward death, increasing the rate and extent of peroxide-triggered programmed cell death. It matters wherever oxidative stress decides cell fate: ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiomyocyte loss, and the removal of cells whose redox damage exceeds repair. The regulators involved act at different levels. FOXO3 is a stress-responsive transcription factor that drives pro-apoptotic and redox target genes, PAWR acts as a pro-apoptotic effector partner, and the mitochondrial nuclease endonuclease G is released to fragment nuclear DNA in a caspase-independent branch of cell death. A microRNA and a forkhead-family transcriptional repressor add post-transcriptional and transcriptional tuning, so sensitivity to peroxide is set by gene expression as much as by the oxidant burden itself.

Zinc is required as a cofactor by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, so cells monitor its availability and remodel transport and gene expression when it runs short. This response to zinc ion starvation adjusts uptake at the cell surface and rewires transcription to preserve the most zinc-dependent functions. Intestinal zinc acquisition depends on SLC39A4, whose loss-of-function causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with dermatitis, diarrhoea and impaired growth, while SLC39A5 contributes to serosal zinc handling and has been linked to myopia and to systemic zinc balance. Downstream, the zinc-finger transcription factor SP1 and the immediate-early factor FOS alter target gene output, including osteoblast products such as osteocalcin and the osteoclast receptor RANK, connecting zinc supply to bone formation and remodelling as well as to epithelial integrity and immune competence.

Cells must sense changes in external osmolarity and respond before they swell or shrink past tolerance, and osmosensory signaling is the route from that physical cue to a corrective response. It matters for systemic water balance, blood pressure control and the volume regulation of every epithelium, and in the kidney and brain it underlies the thirst and vasopressin responses to hypertonicity. Mechanosensitive and osmotically gated cation channels of the TRPV family provide an entry point for calcium, while the WNK-OXSR1 kinase module couples tonicity to phosphorylation of cation-chloride cotransporters and thus to ion and water movement; a sodium channel subunit implicated in sodium-level sensing acts in the same context. Hypotonic or hypertonic stress also converges on the NLRP3 inflammasome with ASC and caspase-1, linking cell volume disturbance to interleukin-1 processing and inflammatory signalling.

When a cell acquires a strongly activating oncogenic lesion, such as mutant HRAS, one outcome is not transformation but a permanent proliferative arrest, and oncogene-induced senescence is that outcome. It acts as a barrier to tumour initiation: cells bearing a driver mutation withdraw irreversibly from the cell cycle, adopt a flattened secretory phenotype, and are often cleared by immune surveillance, so its loss is a recognised step in progression from benign lesion to carcinoma. Arrest is enforced through cell cycle inhibitors including p21, while PML bodies act as organising sites for senescence-associated signalling and architectural HMGA proteins help remodel chromatin into the heterochromatic foci that lock down proliferative genes. Lineage factors such as SPI1 connect the state to transcriptional reprogramming. The programme overlaps replicative and stress-induced senescence but is triggered by oncogenic signalling rather than telomere attrition.

Cells must match their output of cholesterol and fatty acids to demand, and this regulatory layer sets how strongly SREBP transcription factors are allowed to drive that lipogenic programme. Control is exerted mainly on the precursor's escape from the endoplasmic reticulum: INSIG1 and INSIG2 retain the SREBP cleavage-activating protein complex in the ER when sterols are abundant, blocking transport to the Golgi where proteolytic activation occurs, while SPRING1 and scaffolding proteins such as PAQR3 and TMED2 influence trafficking and complex assembly. Additional restraint comes after activation, with the ubiquitin ligase machinery including AMFR and FBXW7 promoting turnover of the mature nuclear form, and microRNA and transcriptional inputs tuning component levels. Loss of this restraint drives unchecked de novo lipogenesis and cholesterol accumulation, linking the pathway to hepatic steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and the lipid supply of proliferating tumour cells.
